title: YOU SAY YOU LOVE GOD… BUT WHAT IF JESUS IS THE HUNGRY PERSON YOU KEEP WALKING PAST?
paragraphs: YOU SAY YOU LOVE GOD… BUT WHAT IF JESUS IS THE HUNGRY PERSON YOU KEEP WALKING PAST?

The frightening truth about a faith that sings to heaven while ignoring suffering on earth—and why the person you refuse to see may reveal more about your relationship with Christ than a thousand Sunday services.
He was sitting outside the church gate when the worship service ended.
His shirt was dirty. His sandals were worn almost beyond repair. His hands trembled slightly as he held an empty plastic cup.
He wasn't asking for much.
Just something to eat.
Inside the church, hundreds of voices had just finished singing about the goodness of God. Hands had been raised. Tears had fallen. People had declared their love for Jesus with everything they had.
And now the service was over.
A man stepped outside, still humming the worship song.
He noticed the hungry stranger.
Their eyes met.
For one uncomfortable second, the man hesitated.
Then he reached into his pocket, pulled out his phone, and pretended to be busy.
He walked past.
The hungry man lowered his eyes.
And somewhere in the silence between those two human beings, a question remained unanswered.
What if the Jesus you were just worshiping inside was calling you to love someone outside?
Before you become angry at that question, understand something.
This isn't merely a story about a man outside a church.
It's about the moments when our declarations of love collide with opportunities to demonstrate it.
It's about the homeless person we avoid making eye contact with.
The elderly neighbor whose refrigerator is almost empty.
The single mother quietly skipping meals so her children can eat.
The struggling family whose smiles conceal a desperate prayer for provision.
The person who never asks for help because humiliation has already taken too much from them.
And sometimes, painfully, it's about us.
Because we can become so familiar with talking about Jesus that we forget what following Him actually requires.
And the most disturbing part?
Jesus warned us about this long before we ever learned how to build beautiful churches, organize worship conferences, or post Bible verses online.
In Matthew 25:35, Jesus declares:
“For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me.” (ESV)
Read that again.
He did not merely say that feeding the hungry was a respectable religious activity.
He identified Himself with those who were suffering.
And when the righteous asked when they had seen Him hungry, thirsty, or in need, He answered:
“As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40, ESV)
That should make every Christian stop for a moment.
Not because every hungry stranger is literally Jesus in disguise.
The passage does not teach that.

In Matthew 25, the expression “my brothers” has a significant interpretive connection to those who belong to Christ, and Christians differ over whether its immediate reference is specifically Jesus' disciples or more broadly people in need.
But the moral force cannot be escaped.

Jesus takes the treatment of vulnerable people seriously. He identifies Himself with His people, especially when they are suffering, and the rest of Scripture repeatedly commands His followers to show practical compassion to those in need.
The King of heaven cares about what happens to people whom the world considers insignificant.
And if the King cares, how can His people remain indifferent?
There is something deeply unsettling about a Christianity that can afford expensive religious celebrations but somehow cannot find room in its heart for a hungry neighbor.
Something is wrong when we can spend freely on our comforts but always have a reason why helping someone else must wait.
Something is wrong when we speak passionately about the love of God while treating human suffering as an inconvenience.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing about that contradiction is how easily we learn to live with it.
We become experts at explaining our inaction.
“They should get a job.”
“They might misuse the money.”
“Someone else will help.”
“I already give to the church.”
“I have my own problems.”
Sometimes those concerns involve real questions of wisdom, safety, responsibility, and stewardship.
Scripture does not require us to abandon discernment or pretend every request is honest.
But there is a difference between exercising wisdom and using suspicion as an excuse to extinguish compassion.
There is a difference between being unable to help and being unwilling even to care.
And God sees the difference.
In the original Greek of 1 John 3:17, the apostle writes:
The verse asks, in essence:
If someone possesses the resources needed for life, sees a fellow believer in need, and closes their heart against that person, how can God's love remain in them?
The Greek expression κλείσῃ τὰ σπλάγχνα (kleisē ta splanchna) is especially striking.
It conveys the act of shutting one's inward compassion.
The word splanchna refers literally to inward parts and figuratively to deep affection or compassion.
John is not simply describing someone who lacks spare money.
He is confronting someone who sees another person's need and deliberately closes the door of compassion.
Think about that.
The tragedy is not only that the needy person remains hungry.
It is that the person with the opportunity to love has begun shutting down something that should be alive within a follower of Jesus.
And John continues:
“Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.” (1 John 3:18, ESV)
Not merely in beautiful captions.
Not merely in emotional worship.
Not merely in the language of Christianity.
In deed.
In truth.
In love that becomes visible.
Now imagine a mother standing in a grocery store.
She has counted her money three times.
Rice. Eggs. Milk.
She cannot afford all three.
Her little boy points toward a small packet of biscuits.
“Mommy, can we get this?”
She smiles.
“Maybe next time.”
He doesn't know that she has already decided not to eat dinner.
He doesn't know that the smile on her face is holding back tears.
He doesn't know that she prayed that morning, asking God to help her make it through another day.
And perhaps, just a few steps away, another Christian is choosing between two things they don't really need.
This is not an accusation against everyone who has more.
Having resources is not itself a sin.
The Bible includes faithful people who possessed wealth and used it for good.
The question is not whether God has allowed something into our hands.
The question is whether His love has reached our hearts.
Because sometimes the answer to someone's prayer begins with a believer who notices.
A bag of groceries.
A warm meal.
A discreet payment for medicine.
An offer to help someone find work.
A phone call that says, “I heard things have been difficult. How can I help?”
Not every act of love requires money.
But genuine love rarely remains content with doing nothing when meaningful help is possible.
James confronts this with almost unbearable clarity.

“If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, be warmed and filled,’ without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?” (James 2:15–16, ESV)
Imagine looking into the eyes of someone who hasn't eaten and saying, “God bless you.”
Then walking away when you could have helped.
James is not attacking prayer.
Prayer is essential.
He is exposing the emptiness of religious words when we use them as substitutes for obedience.
Sometimes the most faithful thing you can do after praying for someone's daily bread is to share the bread God has already placed in your hands.
And here is where the story becomes even more personal.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to be the hungry person.
Perhaps you have stood in a grocery aisle pretending to compare prices when the truth was that you couldn't afford anything.
Perhaps you have watched your children eat while telling them you weren't hungry.
Perhaps you have borrowed money with trembling hands.
Perhaps you have prayed for provision and wondered why heaven seemed silent.
Perhaps someone once looked at your suffering and decided you weren't worth the inconvenience.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Your poverty does not make you less valuable to God.
Your empty wallet does not mean your faith has failed.
Your struggle is not proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
And needing help does not make you a burden unworthy of love.
The Gospel does not belong exclusively to people whose lives are comfortable.
Jesus Himself knew hunger.
After forty days of fasting in the wilderness, Matthew 4:2 tells us that He was hungry.
He knew exhaustion.
He knew rejection.
He knew what it meant to be misunderstood, betrayed, and abandoned.
And at the cross, the Son of God entered the deepest suffering to accomplish our redemption.
He did not come to save only the respectable, the successful, or the financially secure.
He came to seek and save the lost.
And the grace that rescues sinners also begins transforming the way rescued sinners treat one another.
That is why the early church's generosity was so remarkable.
Acts 2:44–45 describes believers sharing their possessions and distributing resources according to people's needs.
Acts 4:34–35 likewise portrays believers making provision so that needs within their community were addressed.
Their generosity was not a method of purchasing salvation.
It was the fruit of a community transformed by the risen Christ.
People who had received extraordinary mercy began extending mercy to others.
People who had been welcomed by grace began opening their lives.
People who knew that Jesus had given Himself for them began asking what they could give for the good of others.
And this is where we must be very careful.
Because even an article about generosity can become spiritually dangerous if it turns the grace of God into a financial transaction.
You cannot buy God's love.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot give enough money to erase a single sin.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9, ESV)
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
His perfect life.
His sacrificial death.
His victorious resurrection.
His mercy toward sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And yet Ephesians does not stop at verse 9.
Verse 10 tells us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Not saved by good works.
Saved for a life in which good works become the evidence of His transforming grace.
That distinction changes everything.
We do not feed the hungry to convince Jesus to love us.
We feed the hungry because we have encountered the love of Jesus.
We do not give to earn the cross.
We give because the cross has revealed a generosity beyond anything we could ever repay.
And we do not show compassion to make ourselves look holy.
We show compassion because Christ is teaching us to see people through His eyes.
There is a beautiful Hebrew word that helps us understand the character of the God we worship.
חֶסֶד — ḥesed.
It is often translated as steadfast love, lovingkindness, mercy, or covenant faithfulness, depending on the context.
In Micah 6:8, God calls His people to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with Him.
The Hebrew phrase וְאַהֲבַת חֶסֶד (we’ahavat ḥesed) expresses the call to love steadfast kindness or mercy.
Notice that God does not merely command outward religious performance.
He calls His people to love what reflects His character.
To love mercy.
Not reluctantly tolerate it.
Not perform it for applause.
Love it.
Because mercy is not an embarrassing interruption to Christian living.
Mercy belongs at its very heart.
And yet we need to confront another painful truth.
Sometimes we are more comfortable funding the appearance of ministry than participating in the costly work of love.
We love impressive stages.
Beautiful graphics.
Powerful music.
Large gatherings.
Inspirational messages.
There is nothing inherently wrong with these things.
They can serve worthy purposes.
But none of them can replace obedience.
A church can have excellent production and still need to examine how it cares for the vulnerable.
A Christian page can have thousands of followers and still need to remember that the people behind the screens are human beings, not numbers.
A ministry can grow in visibility while needing to grow equally in humility, integrity, accountability, and compassion.
And a person can share a thousand Bible verses without allowing a single one to challenge their selfishness.
Jesus did not command us to build an impressive image of Christianity.
He commanded us to love.
“By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:35, ESV)
That love is not sentimental decoration.
It is evidence.
It is costly.
It makes room.
It notices.
It serves.
It sometimes inconveniences us.
And it refuses to reduce another person's suffering to background noise.
Now picture the church gate again.
The worship service has ended.
The hungry man is still sitting outside.
But this time, someone stops.
Not a wealthy person.
Not a famous preacher.
Just an ordinary believer carrying a small bag of food.
“Have you eaten today?”
The man shakes his head.
“Not yet.”
The believer sits beside him.
Not standing over him like a superior person.
Not turning the moment into a public performance.
Not pulling out a camera to collect praise.
Just sitting beside him.
They share a meal.
They talk.
The stranger finally smiles.
And for a moment, something beautiful happens.
The person who was invisible becomes seen.
The person who was dismissed becomes heard.
The person who had been treated like an inconvenience is reminded that he has dignity.
That meal may not solve every problem in his life.
He may still need shelter, medical care, employment, friendship, or long-term support.
But love has taken its first step.
And sometimes the first step is the one that breaks the power of indifference.
There is a reason Jesus told the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke 10:25–37.
A wounded man lay beside the road.
Religious figures passed him.
But a Samaritan, someone whom Jesus' original audience might not have expected to be the hero, stopped and showed mercy.
He approached the wounded man.
He treated his injuries.
He transported him to safety.
He paid for his care.
Jesus then asked which person had proved to be a neighbor.
The answer was the one who showed mercy.
And Jesus said:
“You go, and do likewise.” (Luke 10:37, ESV)
That command still confronts us.
Because the question is not simply, “Who deserves to be my neighbor?”
The question becomes, “Am I willing to become a neighbor to the person who needs mercy?”
Even when they look different.
Even when their life is complicated.
Even when they cannot repay us.
Even when nobody will applaud.
Especially then.
Maybe you're reading this with a strange heaviness in your chest.
You remember someone.
A face.
A voice.
A moment when you could have helped but chose not to.
Maybe you were afraid.
Maybe you were distracted.
Maybe you were tired.
Maybe you simply didn't want to be bothered.
And now that memory is returning.
Do not mistake conviction for hopelessness.
The purpose of biblical conviction is not to convince you that you are beyond God's mercy.
It is to call you out of sin and back toward the Savior.
There is forgiveness for selfishness.
There is forgiveness for indifference.
There is forgiveness for religious pride.
There is forgiveness for the moments when we loved our comfort more than our neighbor.
But forgiveness is not an invitation to remain unchanged.
It is an invitation to repent and walk in a new direction.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind and turning away from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling guilty for a few minutes.
It is a response to God's truth that bears fruit in a changed life.
Remember Zacchaeus?
He was a wealthy tax collector, despised by many because of the abuses associated with his profession.
When Jesus came into his life, something changed.
In Luke 19:8, Zacchaeus declared that he would give half his possessions to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
Jesus did not teach that Zacchaeus purchased salvation through a generous donation.
His changed relationship with money was a visible expression of the transformation taking place in his life.
The man who had been known for taking began to give.
The man associated with exploitation began to pursue restitution.
The man whose story seemed defined by scandal encountered the grace of Jesus Christ.
And grace began rewriting his story.
Not because his past suddenly became acceptable.
Not because his wrongs no longer mattered.
But because the mercy of Christ was powerful enough to bring repentance, restoration, and a new direction.
And perhaps that is the miracle some of us need today.
Not another emotional moment that disappears by tomorrow.
Not another promise to become more compassionate someday.
But a real turning.
A decision.
A phone call.
A meal shared.
A family remembered.
A neighbor visited.
A heart reopened.
Maybe you cannot feed a hundred people.
Feed one if you can.
Maybe you cannot solve poverty in your city.
Help one person take a meaningful step toward stability.
Maybe you have no money to give.
Offer your time, your skills, your encouragement, your advocacy, your prayer, or your willingness to connect someone with trustworthy assistance.
Maybe you are the one struggling financially.
Then receive help without shame when it is offered in love.
The kingdom of God is not a competition over who can give the most.
And Christian generosity should never become a spectacle where people with little are pressured to sacrifice necessities while people with much receive applause for giving what costs them nothing.
Paul writes:
God does not ask you to pretend you possess resources you do not have.
And in 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul teaches that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That matters.
Especially when ministries invite financial support.

Because supporting Gospel-centered work can be a meaningful expression of stewardship, but it must never be presented as a payment for God's favor or a compulsory test of whether someone truly loves Him.
Your giving should be informed.
Prayerful.
Voluntary.
Responsible.
Rooted in love rather than fear.
There is an invitation to participate in a mission.
And if you choose to participate financially, do so freely, with a clear conscience, and with the desire to glorify Christ rather than impress people.
These products are not instruments of salvation, nor can any purchase bring you closer to God by itself.
They are simply resources and expressions of encouragement that may serve your walk with Christ.
That library is part of a larger conviction: biblical nourishment should not be reserved only for people who can afford to pay.
If you are not, you are still welcome.
The invitation to grow in Christ remains.
And there is another way to help that costs nothing.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because someone in your circle may need this reminder today.
Perhaps a believer has become comfortable with a faith that never leaves the church building.
Perhaps someone has been wounded by religious hypocrisy and needs to see that Jesus Himself condemned empty religious performance.
Perhaps a struggling parent needs to know that being poor does not make them forgotten by God.
Perhaps a person who has been blessed with abundance needs encouragement to use that blessing with wisdom and mercy.
You don't have to disclose private details or explain your suffering to strangers.
Sometimes a few words are enough to remind a community that there are real people behind the screens.
Someone else may need to hear that compassion is still alive.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to make people dependent on a page.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
And that brings us back to the question we began with.
Can you claim to love God while ignoring the hungry person outside your door?
The apostle John gives us a searching warning:
“Whoever loves God must also love his brother.” (1 John 4:21, ESV)
And 1 John 4:20 warns against claiming to love God while hating a brother.
John's immediate concern is love within the family of believers, but Scripture's broader witness also calls us to love our neighbors, show hospitality, practice mercy, and care for those in distress.
We must not pretend that one missed opportunity proves a person has never known Christ.
We are finite.
We cannot meet every need.
Sometimes we lack resources, sometimes we must establish boundaries, and sometimes the wisest response is to help through reliable people or organizations.
But a settled, unrepentant indifference toward human suffering is incompatible with the love that Christ commands His followers to cultivate.
The question is not whether you have ever failed to help.
We all have sinned and fallen short of God's glory.
The question is what you will do when God's Word exposes the condition of your heart.
Will you defend your indifference?
Or will you bring it to Jesus?
Will you keep searching for excuses?
Or will you ask Him to teach you compassion?
Will you remain satisfied with appearing religious?
Or will you surrender to the Savior who makes dead hearts alive?
Because Christianity is not merely a collection of correct statements about God.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ, producing a life increasingly shaped by His truth and love.
The hungry person outside your door is not a prop in your spiritual journey.
They are a human being made in the image of God.
They have a name.
A history.
A story.
Fears you may never understand.
Dreams that poverty may have interrupted.
And dignity that no circumstance can erase.
They do not exist merely to test your generosity.
They deserve to be treated with compassion because they are human.
And the Lord who commands us to love our neighbors is the same Lord who loved us when we were helpless to save ourselves.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (ESV)
There is the center of everything.
Not our generosity.
His.
Not our goodness.
His.
Not our ability to earn acceptance.
His finished work on the cross.
Jesus did not wait for us to become worthy before extending mercy.
He came into our brokenness.
He bore our sin.
He died.
He rose again.
And now He calls sinners everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
When that grace truly takes hold of a life, it does not leave our hands, priorities, and relationships untouched.
It teaches us to love because we have first been loved.
It teaches us to forgive because we have been forgiven.
It teaches us to give because we have received more mercy than we could ever deserve.
And it teaches us to see people whom the world has learned to ignore.
So tonight, before you go to sleep, ask yourself one question.
Not, “Did people think I was a good Christian today?”
Not, “How many people liked my Bible post?”
Not, “Did I sound spiritual enough?”
Ask this:
“Lord Jesus, whose suffering have I become too comfortable walking past?”
Then listen to what Scripture has already made clear.
And when an opportunity comes, respond with the wisdom, humility, and compassion Christ is growing in you.
Because somewhere tonight, a child is going to bed hungry.
Somewhere, an elderly person is eating alone.
Somewhere, a father is wondering how to provide for his family.
Somewhere, a mother is praying through tears.
Somewhere, a stranger is hoping someone will notice.
You cannot reach them all.
But you may be able to reach someone.
And that someone is not insignificant to God.
One day, our beautiful buildings, impressive achievements, public recognition, and carefully constructed reputations will no longer matter the way they do now.
What will matter is whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
And a life belonging to Him is called to bear the fruit of His love.
Not perfectly.
Not for applause.
Not to earn salvation.
But because grace changes people.
So don't allow this to become just another article that made you emotional for a moment.
Let it move you toward Christ.
Let it lead you to repentance where repentance is needed.
Let it remind you of the mercy you have received.
And let that mercy become visible in the way you treat the next person who needs your help.
The hungry stranger at the gate may never know your name.
The struggling mother may never be able to repay you.
The lonely neighbor may never tell anyone what you did.
But love does not need an audience to be real.
And the God who sees what is done in secret is never blind to genuine mercy.
Because the most heartbreaking tragedy is not that someone was hungry outside your door—it is that your heart could become so accustomed to their hunger that you no longer heard them knocking.
